title: Everyday Math and Numeracy
summary: By the end, learners can describe official numeracy skills, do everyday calculations and estimates, compare grocery value using unit prices, read gross and net pay as numbers on a stub, and check whether an answer makes sense.
goals: By the end, learners can describe official numeracy skills, do everyday calculations and estimates, compare grocery value using unit prices, read gross and net pay as numbers on a stub, and check whether an answer makes sense.

lessons.title: What numeracy is
lessons.html:
Numeracy is more than school math. The Government of Canada’s Skills for Success model defines it as the ability to find, understand, use, and report mathematical information presented through words, numbers, symbols, and graphics. Official examples include performing calculations, making estimations, and making sense of numbers you see in daily life.

The official skill has clear steps:

  1. Know what question you need to answer.
  2. Find the useful numbers (you may need to scan a bill, a label, or a table).
  3. Connect the pieces of information.
  4. Calculate, put things in order, measure, or estimate.
  5. Check whether the result makes sense.
  6. Share the result if someone else needs it — in writing, in a table, or by speaking.

A Government of Canada numeracy self-assessment (written for the earlier Essential Skills framework, and still posted) lists everyday tasks such as adding and subtracting, making change, adding up a bill, taking simple measurements, comparing sizes or amounts, recording time, estimating quantities, calculating percentages, and comparing similar products to see which is better value.

This course practises those number skills. It does not tell you how to manage debt, choose a loan, or make a household budget, even though some official lists mention budgets as a numeracy task. For money-product rules, use official FCAC pages later or ask a qualified person.

Bring a calculator if it helps — knowing which numbers to use still matters.

lessons.title: Everyday calculations
lessons.html:
The numeracy self-assessment includes simple addition and subtraction, multiplication and division, receiving cash and making change, and calculating the cost of items on a bill.

Add when you combine amounts. If three items cost $2.50, $1.25, and $3.00, the bill is $6.75.

Subtract when you find a difference or make change. If the bill is $6.75 and the customer pays with $10.00, the change is $3.25.

Multiply when the same amount repeats. If one box costs $4 and you buy 3 boxes, that is 3 × $4 = $12.

Divide when you split an amount or find a rate. If 4 people share a $12 cost equally, each person pays $3.

Skills for Success says to check whether the answer has the expected size. A $6.75 bill cannot have $100 in change from a $10 bill. If your answer looks far too big or too small, calculate again.

Write units beside numbers when you can ($ , kg, hours) so you do not add hours to dollars by mistake.

The Canada.ca Content Style Guide writes a percent with a symbol, such as 20%. Lesson 4 practises percentages.

Work slowly on paper or with a calculator. Being careful is part of numeracy, not a weakness.

lessons.title: Measure, compare, and estimate
lessons.html:
The numeracy self-assessment includes taking simple measurements (for example length, weight, or temperature), making comparisons (taller or shorter, heavier or lighter, greater than or less than), recording time, estimating quantities (for example “I need approximately 20 copies”), and estimating measurements. It also lists measurement conversions, such as inches to centimetres or millilitres to litres.

You do not need special tools for every task. A kitchen scale, a wall clock, a vehicle display in kilometres, or a weather report in °C can all be measurement sources. When you must convert one unit to another, look up the official factor or use the scale already printed on the tool. This course does not invent conversion numbers.

Estimate when an exact number is not needed yet. If you need about 20 copies, you do not count them to the last sheet before you start — but you still check later if the exact count matters.

Compare two numbers before you decide. Which package is heavier? Which waiting time is shorter? Which total is greater?

Skills for Success says to judge whether a result is about the right size. If you estimate “about 20 minutes” for a five-minute walk you make every day, the estimate is probably too high. Adjust and try again.

Write down the unit (°C, kg, km, minutes) so other people can use your number.

lessons.title: Percentages and unit prices
lessons.html:
The numeracy self-assessment includes calculating percentages and comparing similar products with different cost structures to determine the best value.

A percentage is a number out of 100. 10% of 80 is 8, because 10 out of every 100 parts of 80 is 8. 50% of a price is half of it. 25% of $40 is $10. If a sign says 20% off a $20 item, you take off $4, so the reduced price is $16 (before any tax that a store may add). This course will not tell you which tax rate applies where you live.

The Office of Consumer Affairs (a Government of Canada office) explains per unit pricing: the price of a product using one set unit, often by weight (kilogram or gram) or volume (litre or millilitre), or sometimes per item. That makes it easier to compare two packages that are different sizes. Cereal boxes can look the same size but hold different amounts.

The same page says unit pricing is required in Quebec. In the rest of Canada, including Alberta, many stores show it voluntarily, but they do not all display it the same way, and the unit price may be in smaller print. A “sale” price is not always the better value — compare the price per kilogram or per litre when you can.

This is shopping numeracy, not advice to buy or avoid a brand.

lessons.title: Numbers on a pay stub
lessons.html:
The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) has a page on starting a first job. It notes that reading a pay stub can be confusing and that most stubs show pay before and after deductions.

Gross pay is the amount before taxes and other payroll deductions. FCAC says it may also include commissions, bonuses, vacation pay, or overtime.

Net pay (take-home pay) is the amount after those deductions. FCAC says this is the amount deposited to a bank account or written on a paycheque.

Your employer may deduct income tax, Employment Insurance (EI), and Canada Pension Plan (CPP) or Quebec Pension Plan (QPP) contributions, and sometimes other amounts such as benefits, savings-plan contributions, or union dues. This course will not tell you how much tax you should pay, whether you qualify for EI, or how to file a return. For SIN and CRA My Account navigation, see the existing LearnHere course on that topic.

Numeracy practice on a stub:

  • Find the gross amount and the net amount.
  • Check that net is smaller than gross (if there were deductions).
  • If you are paid by the hour, multiply hours × hourly rate and see whether that matches the regular-pay line (ask payroll if it does not).

FCAC also writes about budgets, debt, and savings on that page. Those money decisions are outside this course. Use official FCAC tools later if you want money-management information, or ask a qualified person.
